text: Subscribe to skip adsAdvertisementEvolutionThis Prehistoric Alaskan Camp is Rewriting the History of BeringiaStone tools point to a common cultureJCBy Jake Currie1:01 PM CDT on October 14, 2026Add Nautilus to GoogleWhen and how prehistoric humans came to the Americas has been the subject of some heated debate. For the latter half of the 20th century, it was thought that the Clovis people arrived first around 13,000 years ago. Beginning in the 1990s, the discovery of a slew of older sites—some as far south as Chile—seemed to upend that theory. Now a new study published in Science Advances is providing new fodder for debate—as well as some intriguing common threads between pre-Clovis and Clovis cultures.   A team of archeologists conducted a comprehensive survey of an ancient human settlement called Shég’ Xdaltth’í’ (pronounced shehg xuh-tuhl-TTH’EE) in Alaska Native Athabascan (which means “they were here”). The 13,800-year-old settlement is located on a windy bluff overlooking the Tanana River Valley in central Alaska, part of a vital corridor for prehistoric humans making their way through Beringia. The researchers conducted radiocarbon dating of the oldest sediment layer, analyzed the remains of plants and animals found there, and examined a staggering number of artifacts—more than 80,000 altogether. Read more: “The Greatest Journey of All Time”Subscribe to skip adsAdvertisement
